newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Underground punk culture worries Malaysian leaders.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Underground punk culture worries Malaysian leaders.

text.p: "I was once a punkette," Marina Mahathir, daughter of Malaysia's Prime Minister confessed in a recent opinion piece in a local newspaper.

Not for the first time, one senses, that she was at odds with her father. The 71-year-old Mahathir Mohamad has been lamenting the spread of punk culture in Malaysia as a witless aping of "dumb Western culture".
Speaking at a university campus in his home state of Kedah in January, Mahathir could not understand why young Malaysians "put glue on their hair so they look like Red Indians".
"We don't need punk culture. It is stupid," he said.
Education Minister Najib Abdul Razak put his oar in soon afterward, saying on a local television programme punk-style spiky or multi-hued hair would be banned in schools.
He did not mention that Malaysian schools have long enforced strict dress and hairstyle codes.
Clearly, punks have arrived here in a big way. Or not.

Local newspapers have deployed teams of journalists, but sightings of punks and "skinheads" in Malaysia's capital are reportedly as rare as the elusive hornbill, the rainforest bird whose own punk-shaped crown tourists flock to see.
In her essay, Marina explained she dressed up as a punkette, "complete with chains and black eyeliner" for her 19th birthday party at Britain's University of Sussex in 1976.
PUNKS, HIPPIES, MODS AND ROCKERS

"Anything that could so easily become a matter of costuming could not possibly have staying power," she wrote in The Star newspaper in mid-January. "We are having a kerfuffle about punks 20 years too late."
Popular talk show host Patrick Teoh agreed. "It's more of a fashion statement than an ideological one," he told Reuters. "I haven't seen any punks in Kuala Lumpur. What's all the fuss?"

It's all very "retro", a word bandied about by Kuala Lumpur disc jockeys. From retrogressive, it means youth taking their inspirations for fashion, music, the zeitgeist in general, from the counterculture of another age -- punks, hippies, even the mods and rockers of an earlier generation.
Some 60,000 Malaysians study abroad, mostly in Britain, the United States and Australia. They apparently are bringing back their extracurricular experiences along with their degrees.
In Malaysia, the underground scene also features hip-hop rappers, reggae rastafarians, acid rockers, grunge and heavy metal artists. Pubs like the Hip-P in Kuala Lumpur cater to the different groups.
But the authorities link the underground with darker things -- drugs, alcohol abuse and a rise in teenage gang violence.
Days after the Prime Minister made his punk pronouncements, Kuala Lumpur ordered the city's 477 pubs and amusement centres to close by 1 a.m., an hour or two earlier than before.
At the same time, narcotics police made a series of drug raids against the more notorious teenage hangouts, rounding up hundreds of youths and administering urine tests.
Deputy Home Minister Megat Junid Megat Ayob said Mahathir launched the campaign after a leadership council meeting of his United Malays National Organisation on January 11.
Some entertainment centres were dens of promiscuity and drug abuse and Mahathir viewed them as "the root of all social problems", Megat Junid told reporters last Sunday.
TEENAGE GANG VIOLENCE
The campaign has coincided with official concerns over an increase in teenage gang violence associated with Chinese "secret societies", such as the triads.
The Malay-language Utusan Malaysia triggered the punk debate with a series of articles in January about how young ethnic Malays are joining punk and skinhead groups.
The government is particularly worried about what it views as negative trends among Malays, the majority ethnic group in multi-racial Malaysia.

Labour-short Malaysia is trying to move up the technology ladder and away from the labour-intensive assembly industries that are now the backbone of the manufacturing sector. An educated labour force is key to that strategy, analysts say.

Punk culture took root among the working class in Britain of the 1970s, in reaction against the peace-and-love hippie scene of the 1960s. Like the hippies they held in contempt, punks aimed to shock mainstream culture with their appearance, in this case safety pins stuck in their faces, Mohawk hairstyles, torn jeans and leather clothes.
Skinheads, often associated with quasi-fascist sentiments, became a subculture in the 1980s. Kuala Lumpur has a few, who say they share the look but not the ideology.
"We don't beat up people," a 15-year-old Kuala Lumpur skinhead identified as "Fas" told the New Straits Times.
"We don't practise anarchy or even believe in white supremacy.
"It's the music and the looks. It's just for effect."
